Q55347059.summary: Only fragments remain of this silk banner, but a haloed figure in three-quarter view can still be made out, wearing a red stole over a robe that has faded almost to the colour of the silk, with small flowers scattered across the background. Crosses appear on his headdress, on a pendant at his chest and at the head of a staff, marking him as Christian although the pose and gestures recall Buddhist bodhisattva images. Found in the Library Cave at Dunhuang, it is a rare witness to the Church of the East in China and may represent Christ himself.
facts: The painting was recovered by Aurel Stein in 1908 from the Library Cave (Cave 17) of the Mogao Caves and is now in the British Museum.
The figure's red moustache and beard, rather than the green curling moustaches typical of bodhisattvas, are among the features that point to a Christian rather than Buddhist subject.
Scholars including Hans-Joachim Klimkeit and Christoph Baumer describe it as Christ or a saint, while others such as P. Y. Saeki and Tōru Haneda regarded it as an image of Christ.

Q55347059.notes: Identification uncertain: the figure may be Christ or a Christian saint. Much of the detail described in sources (beard, crosses) is hard to see in this heavily damaged photograph. Scripture omitted because the subject is not certain.

cur:catacombs-louvre-livia-primitiva.summary: Between bands of strigils, a simple incised panel names Livia Primitiva, who died aged 24 years and 9 months, and below it shows the Good Shepherd with a sheep on his shoulders between two others, accompanied by a fish and an anchor. Modest as it is, it is one of the earliest objects to declare its owner's Christian faith openly.
facts: Its inscription records that Livia Nicarus made it for her sister Livia Primitiva.
Commons notes that the Good Shepherd, the fish and the anchor together show that the deceased belonged to the Christian community.
cur:catacombs-louvre-livia-primitiva.notes: The Good Shepherd is a symbolic image of Christ; here the fish and anchor make the Christian reading clear.

cur:catacombs-arles-paulus-geminus.summary: Three arches on columns frame the scene: at the centre Christ, bearded and nimbed with a cross above, stands with arms outstretched, while two apostles approach from either side, one carrying a cross. Reused as an altar front, the sarcophagus still sets Christ in glory above the altar.
facts: It was made for Paulus Geminus, administrator of the treasury of the Five Provinces of Gaul, according to the Commons description.
It now supports the altar of the Chapel of the Holy Sepulchre in the former cathedral of Saint-Trophime.
cur:catacombs-arles-paulus-geminus.notes: The central figure's identification as Christ is clear from the cross; the side figures are probably Peter and Paul.

vam:O88288.summary: In the upper scene Christ rides into Jerusalem on an ass, followed by two disciples, while the people of the city, waving palm branches, spread their garments on the ground before him. Below, he sits at table with his apostles in the house of Simon as a woman kneels to anoint his feet, the meal laid out on a draped table between them. The deeply carved, animated figures are characteristic of the later Metz ivories.
facts: The back of the plaque carries an earlier carving, probably made in the Alto Adige/South Tyrol in the late 8th or early 9th century, with the Baptism and Ascension of Christ; it was cut down at the top, losing the figure of Christ in the Ascension, when the Metz scenes were carved.
The V&A relates the earlier side stylistically to a diptych in the Musée de Cluny in Paris and to a plaque of Christ in Majesty in the Bayerisches Nationalmuseum, Munich.
It was formerly in the Soltikoff collection (sale 1861) and was bought from the Webb collection.
vam:O88288.notes: The V&A identifies the woman as Mary Magdalene. Obverse: Metz, ca. 870–880; reverse: probably Alto Adige, late 8th–early 9th century.

walters:45.13.summary: This tiny silver medallion, under two centimetres across, is framed by a beaded rim with a small tab for attachment. The side shown in the photograph bears a nielloed bust of the Virgin, veiled and frontal, with letters of her monogram at either side. According to the museum's title, the medallion also carries an image of Christ Pantokrator, presumably on the other face.
facts: The Walters dates the medallion to the 10th century; it measures about 1.9 × 2 cm.
It was given to the museum in 1941 by the Baltimore collector Saidie A. May.
walters:45.13.notes: Only one photograph is available and it shows the Virgin; the image of Christ named in the title cannot be seen or confirmed.
